# Tittirajātaka (Ja 319)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Partridge

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tittirajātaka* (Ja 319) is a narrative within the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. The story opens with the phrase *Susukham vata jīvāmi* ("Happy life") and is set while the Buddha was residing at the Badarika Monastery near Kosambī [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. Its present-day framing concerns the novice or elder Rāhula, whose virtues—being eager for training, scrupulous, and forbearing under rebuke—were being praised by the monks in the Dhamma hall [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883; Ratanamalai 2007]. The Buddha notes that this introductory context corresponds to that related in the *Tipallatthajātaka* and explains that Rāhula possessed these same virtuous qualities in previous existences [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883; Ratanamalai 2007].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was living as an ascetic, while Rāhula was born as a decoy partridge kept in a cage by a bird hunter to lure wild partridges [Fausböll 1883; Crosby 2014]. When the decoy called out, wild partridges approached and were trapped; when it kept silent, the hunter beat it, provoking squawks that still drew wild birds to their capture [Crosby 2014]. Burdened by moral anxiety, the partridge questioned whether it incurred demerit and guilt for the capture of other birds [Fausböll 1883; Crosby 2014]. The Bodhisatta resolved its scruples, explaining that where there is no evil intention in the mind, no sin or fault attaches to the action [Fausböll 1883; Crosby 2014]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the decoy partridge as Rāhula and the ascetic as himself [Fausböll 1883]. This story is distinct from the better-known homonymous *Tittira Jātaka* (Ja 37), which deals with the seniority of a partridge, a monkey, and an elephant [Crosby 2014].

SuttaCentral lists four translations of the text across four modern languages [SuttaCentral]. In terms of text reuse, DharmaNexus identifies six Pali-internal matching passages between this text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Tatiyo bhāgo), with the longest match spanning segments §0.4–1.4 against §490–491 (similarity 0.96) [DharmaNexus]. No cross-language parallels meeting the score threshold of 10 are recorded by DharmaNexus [DharmaNexus].
